newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian prosecutor again seeks life for ex-Nazi.
newsitem.headline: Italian prosecutor again seeks life for ex-Nazi.

text.p: A military prosecutor sought on Friday for the second time to have former Nazi SS captain Erich Priebke sentenced to life for his part in Italy's worst World War Two massacre.

Antonino Intelisano, summing up in a courtroom in Rome's Rebibbia high-security jail, asked for a 24-year term for former SS major Karl Hass, who also faced charges of complicity in the 1944 massacre of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves.
He said Priebke deserved the stiffer sentence because his crimes were aggravated by cruelty, brutality and premeditation.
Both Priebke and Hass have admitted taking part in the massacre, in which the victims, including 75 Jews, were taken to the caves outside Rome and shot in the back of the neck.
Both said they shot two victims each and Priebke also said he checked names off a list, but they argued they were following orders and would have been killed themselves if they disobeyed.
Intelisano said there were sufficient mitigating circumstances in Hass' case to warrant the lighter sentence. He did not elaborate on them.
A former Italian justice minister, Giuliano Vassalli, told the court earlier this month that Hass had helped save his life while he was a prisoner at the Gestapo's Rome headquarters.
Neither Priebke, 83, nor Hass, 84, were in court.
Intelisano said, however, that the age of the defendants should be taken into consideration -- meaning that the two men could be held under house arrest if sentenced by the court.
Priebke, who was extradited from Argentina in November 1995 where he had lived openly for nearly half a century, is being held under house arrest at a Roman Catholic monastery.

Hass appeared as a prosecution witness in Priebke's first trial, which ended in uproar last August. A military court ruled that the German was guilty of complicity in the massacre but could not be punished under a statute of limitations.
Protestors besieged the court and Priebke was re-arrested a few hours later. The verdict was quashed on appeal.

Hass reluctantly testified at the first Priebke trial from a hospital bed after injuring himself while trying to flee from a hotel balcony. He was arrested after admitting in court that he too killed victims and is also being held under house arrest.
Lawyers for the civil plaintiffs were due to make their final summing up in the case at the start of July and the verdict was expected shortly afterwards.
Rome mayor Francisco Rutelli attended the session on Friday saying it was important that war crimes should not be forgotten.
"It's up to the independent magistrature to judge and rule," he told reporters.
"I don't intend to lobby in any way. Mine is a testimony.
"But the city of Rome is not neutral. Half a century has passed but it is still like rubbing salt into a wound that is open and burning."
